disputed: DOJ argues these state actions are preempted by the Clean Air Act and violate the Commerce Clause and federal foreign-affairs power, because states cannot regulate a global problem or impose liability for out-of-state emissions. Those are real legal questions that courts are still resolving. Using the federal government to sue states on behalf of a private industry before they have filed suit is unusual, but that does not make it unlawful.

items: Executive Order 'Protecting American Energy From State Overreach' (April 8, 2025) told DOJ to 'expeditiously take all appropriate action to stop the enforcement' of such state laws. (Hunton (https://www.hunton.com/the-nickel-report/doj-files-suit-against-hawaii-michigan-new-york-and-vermont-related-to-climate-legal-actions))

April 30, 2025: DOJ sued Hawaii and Michigan to block climate lawsuits they had announced against fossil-fuel companies before the states could file them. May 1, 2025: DOJ sued New York and Vermont over their climate-superfund laws, which make large emitters pay for climate damage. (Hunton (https://www.hunton.com/the-nickel-report/doj-files-suit-against-hawaii-michigan-new-york-and-vermont-related-to-climate-legal-actions); E&E News (https://www.eenews.net/articles/doj-sues-to-block-state-climate-superfunds/))

Hawaii filed its suit against the oil companies anyway. (Climate in the Courts (https://www.climateinthecourts.com/hawaii-sues-big-oil-for-alleged-climate-deception-after-trump-administration-tried-to-block-the-litigation/))
sections.label: Documentation

summary: A Trump executive order (April 8, 2025) directed DOJ to stop state laws 'burdening' energy production. Within weeks DOJ sued four states: two to block their climate-superfund laws, and two to preempt climate-deception lawsuits against oil companies that had not yet been filed.
title: DOJ sues states to shield oil companies from climate liability
